construction_notes: Treatment is defined on the CLOSEST universal nurse visit around the recommended vaccination week, counting both scheduled and additional (needs-based) visits.

The recommended vaccination weeks are week 13 (three months round) and week 22 (five months round); each round consists of a combined diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis-polio-Hib vaccination and a pneumococcus vaccination.

Outcomes are weekly indicators (uptake) and their cumulative counterparts (coverage), built from the week of vaccine administration; the paper observes the week, not the day, of administration (footnote 6).
Parental background characteristics are lagged two years prior to the focal child's birth.
Table 1 reports that the estimation samples cover 23 percent (three months) and 20 percent (five months) of all children of the cohorts.

Reference weeks differ by panel: the first week of life for Fig. 5 panel (a), week 15 for Fig. 6 panel (a), and the closest week leading up to the definition of the treatment group for the accumulated-coverage panels.

claims.statement: A universal nurse home visit in the two weeks before the recommended week for the first (three months) vaccination raises the probability that the child receives that vaccination in week 12 of life, the week before the recommended week.

definition.value: Indicator equal to one if the child's single closest universal nurse home visit falls in the two weeks leading up to the week in which the first vaccination round is recommended (week 13) -- i.e. in week 12 or week 13 -- and zero if that visit falls in the two-week period after the recommended week (weeks 14-15). Children are restricted to have only one nurse visit in the four-week window. Mean week of the focal visit is 12.49 in the treatment group and 14.44 in the control group (Table 2).

population.selection: Children with exactly one universal nurse home visit in the four weeks around week 13, the recommended age for the first vaccination round (two weeks before = treated, two weeks after = control); families assigned to nurses with only one assigned family in the sample (one percent) are omitted so that nurse fixed effects can be used. 23 percent of all children of the 2012-2016 cohorts in the 58 municipalities enter this sample.

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in the exact week of the closest universal nurse home visit within the four weeks around week 13, the nationally recommended age for the first infant vaccination round: families visited in the two weeks before that week are compared with families visited in the two weeks after it. The variation arises from visit-to-visit scheduling by nurses and families, which the paper argues does not depend on the recommended vaccination ages.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariate vector X, nurse fixed effects and year-of-birth fixed effects, the timing of the closest-spaced nurse visit within the four-week window is as good as random -- i.e. uncorrelated with other determinants of vaccination uptake (conditional ignorability of treatment timing).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balance table of 21 background characteristics for treatment and control groups (Table 2); event-study pre-trends in non-preventive GP contacts (Fig. 4); regressions of treatment status on all background variables, year-of-birth and nurse fixed effects in which only 2 of 20 variables are significant at 5 percent (footnote 9); random placebo test (Fig. 9).

threats_discussed: Selection on unobservables that the covariates miss: treated families might be more likely to vaccinate anyway (p. 9).
Differences in nurse care across treatment and control groups by construction: treated children have their initial nurse visit earlier and fewer visits before the focal visit (Table 2, p. 7).
Seasonality in births, vacation periods and disease season that could delay both nurse visits and vaccination uptake (footnote 8; month-of-birth robustness test).

Pertussis (whooping cough) incidence influencing both the timing of nurse visits, nurses' focus on vaccination and parents' uptake (robustness test controlling for monthly pertussis hospitalizations).
Nurse quality or nurse emphasis on vaccination (addressed by nurse fixed effects; robustness test replaces them with municipality fixed effects).
Parents scheduling nurse and GP appointments on the same day (argued unlikely; footnote 6 states it cannot be checked empirically).
The 2014 vaccination reminder-letter policy (argued not confounding because letters are sent at age two).
robustness_checks: Wider data window: four weeks on either side of the recommended vaccination week to define treatment and control groups (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Excluding all covariates from the estimation (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Replacing nurse fixed effects with municipality fixed effects (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Adding month-of-birth fixed effects to capture seasonality (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Controlling for the number of pertussis hospitalizations in the recommended vaccination month (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Random placebo test: the week of the closest nurse visit is randomized and the main event study re-estimated 200 times (Fig. 9).
Dropping all families assigned to nurses in the top and bottom one percentiles of the distribution of assigned children per nurse per year (footnote 7, results available on request).
Balance regressions of treatment status on all background variables, year-of-birth and nurse fixed effects (footnote 9).
unresolved_confounders: Potential selection into early-visit status that the controls miss: 'Even if treatment families were more likely to take up the vaccine in the first place (due to potential selection that our controls miss)' (p. 9).
Differences in prior nurse care across treatment and control groups, which 'may also indicate some differences across families' (p. 7).

Whether parents schedule the nurse visit and the vaccination appointment on the same day: footnote 6 states 'we are unable to check this idea empirically as we only observe the date of the nurse visit and the week of the vaccine administration' (p. 4).

ambiguities: The paper gives one magnitude -- 'one percentage point' -- for weeks 12 and 13 together; it is recorded here for week 12 and separately for week 13, distinguished by the paper's own relative magnitudes (25 and 6 percent). Read against the axis, Fig. 5 panel (a) plots roughly 0.008 at week 12 and roughly 0.014 at week 13, so 'one percentage point' is the authors' rounding of two different coefficients.
Statistical significance is read off the plotted 95 percent confidence interval in Fig. 5, panel (a); the paper states no significance level for this coefficient.

threats_discussed: Selection on unobservables that the covariates miss: treated families might be more likely to vaccinate anyway (p. 9).
Differences in nurse care across treatment and control groups by construction: treated children have their initial nurse visit earlier and fewer visits before the focal visit (Table 2, p. 7).
Seasonality in births, vacation periods and disease season that could delay both nurse visits and vaccination uptake (footnote 8; month-of-birth robustness test).

Pertussis (whooping cough) incidence influencing both the timing of nurse visits, nurses' focus on vaccination and parents' uptake (robustness test controlling for monthly pertussis hospitalizations).
Nurse quality or nurse emphasis on vaccination (addressed by nurse fixed effects; robustness test replaces them with municipality fixed effects).
Parents scheduling nurse and GP appointments on the same day (argued unlikely; footnote 6 states it cannot be checked empirically).
The 2014 vaccination reminder-letter policy (argued not confounding because letters are sent at age two).
robustness_checks: Wider data window: four weeks on either side of the recommended vaccination week to define treatment and control groups (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Excluding all covariates from the estimation (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Replacing nurse fixed effects with municipality fixed effects (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Adding month-of-birth fixed effects to capture seasonality (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Controlling for the number of pertussis hospitalizations in the recommended vaccination month (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Random placebo test: the week of the closest nurse visit is randomized and the main event study re-estimated 200 times (Fig. 9).
Dropping all families assigned to nurses in the top and bottom one percentiles of the distribution of assigned children per nurse per year (footnote 7, results available on request).
Balance regressions of treatment status on all background variables, year-of-birth and nurse fixed effects (footnote 9).

Whether parents schedule the nurse visit and the vaccination appointment on the same day: footnote 6 states 'we are unable to check this idea empirically as we only observe the date of the nurse visit and the week of the vaccine administration' (p. 4).

threats_discussed: Selection on unobservables that the covariates miss: treated families might be more likely to vaccinate anyway (p. 9).
Differences in nurse care across treatment and control groups by construction: treated children have their initial nurse visit earlier and fewer visits before the focal visit (Table 2, p. 7).
Seasonality in births, vacation periods and disease season that could delay both nurse visits and vaccination uptake (footnote 8; month-of-birth robustness test).

Pertussis (whooping cough) incidence influencing both the timing of nurse visits, nurses' focus on vaccination and parents' uptake (robustness test controlling for monthly pertussis hospitalizations).
Nurse quality or nurse emphasis on vaccination (addressed by nurse fixed effects; robustness test replaces them with municipality fixed effects).
Parents scheduling nurse and GP appointments on the same day (argued unlikely; footnote 6 states it cannot be checked empirically).
The 2014 vaccination reminder-letter policy (argued not confounding because letters are sent at age two).
robustness_checks: Wider data window: four weeks on either side of the recommended vaccination week to define treatment and control groups (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Excluding all covariates from the estimation (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Replacing nurse fixed effects with municipality fixed effects (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Adding month-of-birth fixed effects to capture seasonality (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Controlling for the number of pertussis hospitalizations in the recommended vaccination month (Appendix Figs. A.9-A.12).
Random placebo test: the week of the closest nurse visit is randomized and the main event study re-estimated 200 times (Fig. 9).
Dropping all families assigned to nurses in the top and bottom one percentiles of the distribution of assigned children per nurse per year (footnote 7, results available on request).
Balance regressions of treatment status on all background variables, year-of-birth and nurse fixed effects (footnote 9).

links.pointer_quote: Our results demonstrate that timely nurse visits have short run effects on parental vaccination uptake: Treated parents have a higher probability of timely uptake of the three and five months vaccinations compared to control parents.
While we find effects on timely vaccination uptake, the overall coverage of the children in the control group catches up with those treated over time.
